findings.location: Section 6D 'Steel-manning the strongest objection' — the closing sentences: "Competing throughput claims exist on both sides without published harnesses ... so no benchmark settles it."
findings.issue: The draft names the strongest alternative (adopt a router that ships non-pod discovery) but suppresses that alternative's single strongest piece of evidence: vLLM's own published benchmark claims the vLLM Router beats llm-d by 25% request throughput and 1200 ms TTFT on Llama 3.1 8B with 8 prefill / 8 decode pods, and matches llm-d's throughput with 2000 ms faster TTFT on DeepSeek V3 (1 prefill TP8 + 1 decode TP8). Reducing that to a symmetric 'claims exist on both sides' is a strawman of the opposing case in a register where steel-man quality is the standard — and it is inconsistent with §5C, which does state llm-d's own vendor numbers in full before attributing them.
findings.evidence: [[vllm-router-a-high-performance-and-prefilldecode-aware-load-balancer-for-large-s]] — quoted: "vLLM Router (blue line) Req/S throughput is 25% higher than llm-d (purple line) ... vLLM Router's TTFT is close to K8s-native load balancer and 1200 ms faster than llm-d." Two mitigants are in the same note and currently unused by the draft: the acknowledgements thank llm-d engineers Tyler Michael Smith and Robert Shaw "for sharing llm-d expertise and receipts which unblocked performance optimizations and benchmarks" (so it is not a third-party benchmark, but it is also not a hostile one), and the benchmark explicitly excluded vLLM's own recommended DP/EP coordinator because its throughput was 1/8 of the others due to vllm-project/vllm#24461 (an incomplete field).
findings.recommendation: In §6D, state the vLLM Router numbers explicitly with the same vendor-reported attribution §5C already applies to llm-d's own figures, then answer rather than elide: note that the benchmark is the vendor's own with llm-d-engineer input and an excluded competitor, that it measures P/D throughput rather than shared-prefix cache affinity (the capability the report says you are buying), and let the reversibility argument in §6E carry the weight. Replace 'no benchmark settles it' with a statement of what the benchmark does and does not bear on.

findings.location: Section 7A 'Four decision rules' (Rule 1 opens with availability) and Section 7B Phases — the procedure never asks whether the estate can be pods; cf. §6C "That is a governance decision and should be made explicitly rather than defaulted past."
findings.issue: The draft concedes in §6C that estate conversion (Slinky) must be decided explicitly, then supplies a decision procedure that defaults past it: Rules 1-4 and Phases 0-4 contain no gate for it, and the ranking demotes it to a parenthetical ('G only if fleet custody is on the table'). This matters more than a normal alternative because, on the user's own framing — 'use llm-d components as much as possible' — conversion is the maximum-reuse option: stock router, stock charts, leader-elected HA, the policy CRDs, PodMonitor scraping, and a functioning sidecar allowlist. The counter-draft made it Gate 1; the final report makes it a footnote on a framing move ('it answers a different question') rather than on evidence.
findings.evidence: research/runs/.../temp/draft-b.md Gate 1; [[running-large-scale-gpu-workloads-on-kubernetes-with-slurm-nvidia-technical-blog]] and [[github-slinkyprojectslurm-operator-run-slurm-on-kubernetes-a-slinky-project-gith]] (production at NVIDIA, >1,000 worker nodes / 8,000+ GPUs, collective-communication performance matching non-containerised Slurm).
findings.recommendation: Insert a short 'Rule 0' (or a Phase 0 prerequisite sentence) in §7A that makes the conversion question the first written decision, with its named criterion (does the organisation accept Kubernetes as the fleet's primary scheduler?) and an explicit note that answering yes maximises llm-d reuse and ends the project. One paragraph; do not restructure §6C.

findings.location: Section 7A, Rule 1 — "If it is, run the picker in-cluster under the Helm chart — leader election over a Lease works normally — while the backend inventory points off-cluster"
findings.issue: The report's recommended answer for any deployment with an availability requirement is the hybrid topology, and it never engages the explicit architectural objection to hybrids that is on disk, nor does it carry §8's own concession ('nobody has published the hybrid shape') to the point of recommendation. A reader following Rule 1 gets the recommendation without either the objection or the undemonstrated-status caveat.
findings.evidence: [[inference-support-agentgateway-as-a-standalone-provider-issue-620-agentgatewayag]] — a maintainer: "I get that but why would they run on Kubernetes without wanting to use Kubernetes APIs. Two things make sense: - All Kubernetes - No Kubernetes. A hybrid of those seems very very odd." Draft-B §4 uses this as a load-bearing objection.
findings.recommendation: After the hybrid branch in Rule 1, add one or two sentences quoting the maintainer objection and answering it on the evidence the draft already holds: the objection is about Gateway API surface, not about discovery, and the chart's raw-config plus extra-volume escape hatches make the shape reachable — while flagging that it remains a capability inference with no published deployment (cross-reference §8's audited absence rather than repeating it).

findings.location: Section 7A, Rule 4 — "Do not assume fail-open off Kubernetes: llm-d's scoped fail-open is tied to a lease-transition window that does not exist without a Lease"
findings.issue: The caution is asserted without acknowledging the documented fact that points the other way: operations.md states router.proxy.failOpen: true is the default in standalone mode, and that with it the proxy passes requests directly to backend model servers without dropping traffic. A reader who checks the docs will find the draft appears to contradict them; the draft's actual (correct) point is narrower — that the lease-transition trigger and the proxy-held endpoint list both vanish off-cluster.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-routerdocsoperationsmd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]] — "With router.proxy.failOpen: true (the default in standalone mode) ... if the active leader crashes or restarts, the proxy passes requests directly to backend model servers without dropping traffic during the lease transition period." comparisons.md Tension 5 flags the no-Kubernetes envoy.yaml failure_mode_allow default as an explicit open check.
findings.recommendation: In Rule 4, name the documented default first, then state precisely why it does not transfer (no Lease to transition, and an ORIGINAL_DST cluster has no member list to fall back to), and mark the shipped envoy.yaml's ext_proc failure-mode setting as the unverified item. Keep the §8 audited-absence sentence as is.

findings.location: Section 5D 'The one component you cannot reuse unchanged' and the §1B inventory row "P/D disaggregation sidecar ... **Yes, with network isolation**"
findings.issue: The carve-out is stated one step short of its actual conclusion. The draft says the allowlist is off by default and describes what it does when enabled, but never states flatly that off Kubernetes it cannot be enabled at all (it takes input exclusively from an InferencePool watch and additionally requires cluster role bindings) — so the sidecar runs permanently in the mode where IsAllowed() returns true unconditionally. The inventory verdict 'Yes, with network isolation' therefore reads softer than the report's own evidence, and the counter-draft's stronger reading ('Only unprotected') goes unanswered. The draft also narrows the exposure to the prefill leg when the handler proxies KV-cache-source and encoder targets on the same unvalidated-header path.
findings.evidence: [[allowlistgo]] (InferencePool + selected pods are the only input paths; no static/CIDR/flag alternative), [[featsidecar-implement-ssrf-protection-with-inferencepool-host-port-allowlist-by]] (cluster role bindings required to enable), [[chat_completionsgo]] (KV-cache-source and encoder targets proxied from headers), comparisons.md Tension 3 carve-out.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence in §5D stating plainly that off Kubernetes the allowlist is not merely off by default but unavailable, so the network-isolation obligation is the entire control rather than a supplement; extend the header-driven exposure to name the KV-cache-source and encoder targets; and sharpen the inventory verdict wording so it does not read as unqualified reuse.

findings.location: Opening thesis paragraph (line 1) — "One carve-out is mandatory ... And one version correction governs day one"
findings.issue: The lede prices two costs (the P/D sidecar, the unreleased config key) but omits the one the body itself calls 'the strongest objection': that taking the recommended escalation (strategy C) makes the reader the first known out-of-tree importer, against an interface reshaped three times in four months, in a framework with no panic recovery on any plugin call path. A committed advocate lede that omits its own strongest counter-cost reads as advocacy rather than as a decision brief, and a reader who stops after the lede is not warned.
findings.evidence: §3C of the draft itself ('The strongest objection, at full strength'); [[framework-define-a-panic-isolation-posture-for-plugin-extension-points-issue-210]]; pkg.go.dev no-known-importers finding recorded in comparisons.md.
findings.recommendation: Add one clause to the lede noting that the escalation rung (a custom plugin) is unprecedented in the wild and priced rather than argued away, pointing forward to §3C. Do not expand it into a paragraph — the lede's committed tone should survive.

findings.location: Section 5E 'The one functional loss' — "Per-request priority via `InferenceObjective` is the single genuine gap."
findings.issue: The absolute claim contradicts the draft's own inventory and §8. The §1B table marks InferenceObjective/InferenceModelRewrite, EPP high availability, peer discovery, and gateway-mode proxies as not reusable; §5D adds the sidecar allowlist; §8's 'The custom surface tends to grow' enumerates a bundle (priority admitter, peer-discovery plugin, hand-authored Envoy config, static Prometheus SD, network isolation). Calling priority 'the single genuine gap' is the one place the draft's own cross-locus tension (comparisons.md Tension 1: 'thin' and 'low-risk' do not survive) is smoothed over.
findings.evidence: comparisons.md Tension 1 ('Locus A costed ONE plugin; the other loci each add a potential second or third custom Go component'); draft §1B table rows; draft §8.
findings.recommendation: Scope the claim: make it 'the one functional loss among the custom-resource-driven policy inputs' (or equivalent), and add a half-sentence pointing at §8's bundle discussion so the reader does not carry away a one-gap picture. Do not delete the section's committed conclusion.

findings.location: Section 7A, Rule 1 closing — "run N pickers Active-Active behind a plain layer-4 load balancer with leader election **explicitly disabled**" and the supporting paragraph citing issue #1290
findings.issue: This is the draft's most consequential inferential leap and it does not state its provenance. The #1290 measurements were taken on a Kubernetes deployment; the report extrapolates them to N picker processes behind an L4 load balancer outside Kubernetes, which nobody has published. Under the run's deep-inference directive, a derived claim must name the sourced claims it derives from, and an audited absence must state what was searched. §8's 'Audited absences' paragraph lists the hybrid shape and precise-routing-plus-file-discovery but not this one.
findings.evidence: [[evaluate-llm-d-router-both-epp-and-the-standalone-proxy-scale-limits-issue-1290]] (in-cluster QPS/latency benchmark, independent synthetic requests), [[cross_replica_syncergo]] (precise extractor does not implement the cross-replica contributor interface — the mechanism that licenses the extrapolation).
findings.recommendation: Add a clause naming the derivation explicitly: the recommendation rests on the code-level mechanism (independent per-endpoint KV-event subscription, no peer synchronisation) plus in-cluster benchmark data, not on any off-cluster measurement — and add off-cluster Active-Active to §8's audited-absence list as a test to run rather than a risk to hedge.

findings.location: Section 7A, Rule 1 supporting paragraph — "precise prefix-cache failures at 500 queries per second fall monotonically as replicas rise: 3,148 failures at one replica, then 57, 31, and 18 at four"
findings.issue: Under-commitment where the evidence supports more. The draft argues the Active-Active branch entirely from a third-party benchmark issue and omits the first-party documentation that most directly supports it: operations.md publishes an Active-Active throughput-scaling table (1.0x / 2.0x / 2.7x / 3.5x at 1-4 replicas) and scopes its own Active-Active warning to approximate prefix routing because replicas do not share prefix state. That is llm-d's own documentation supporting llm-d's own Active-Active mode — stronger than the benchmark and currently unused. The same source also supplies the contrast the draft needs (Active-Passive gives no throughput scaling at all), which is what makes the chart's silent leader-election injection a real trap rather than a nuisance.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-routerdocsoperationsmd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]] — "Active-Active Mode: ... providing near-linear throughput scaling: | 1 | 1.0x | | 2 | 2.0x | | 3 | 2.7x | | 4 | 3.5x |" and "Active-Active mode should be avoided when using approximate prefix routing. Because EPP replicas do not share prefix state..."
findings.recommendation: Insert the documented scaling figures (and the fact that the warning is documented as scoped to approximate routing, quoting the doc rather than characterising it) into the Rule 1 supporting paragraph, ahead of the #1290 data. Pair it with the Active-Passive no-scaling fact so the leader-election-injection trap lands with its cost attached.

findings.location: Section 3C, third move — "wrap your `Start()` goroutine in your own recovery because the framework provides none" (repeated in Phase 3)
findings.issue: The mitigation is stated as if it generalises, but it only works because a discovery plugin's sole call path is Start(). The draft elsewhere contemplates a priority admitter plugin (§5E, §8), which sits on the per-request scheduling path where a recover() in your own start goroutine gives no protection at all. Left unstated, the panic objection looks fully answered; stated, it becomes the sharpest argument for the draft's own 'keep the bundle to one plugin' rule.
findings.evidence: [[framework-define-a-panic-isolation-posture-for-plugin-extension-points-issue-210]] (no plugin invocation anywhere has panic recovery, at any extension point); draft §8 'The custom surface tends to grow'.
findings.recommendation: Add a half-sentence in §3C (or in §8's custom-surface paragraph) noting that self-recovery is adequate for a discovery plugin precisely because Start() is its only call path, and that any request-path plugin you add later is outside that protection — making the one-plugin constraint a safety property, not just a cost control.

findings.location: Section 8, 'Multi-replica caveats' — "the picker's idle CPU grows with the number of model servers it scrapes, and on Kubernetes those numbers arrive as a resource block the chart writes for you"
findings.issue: The concession is made without the numbers that are on disk, which makes it read as a gesture rather than a cost. The counter-draft used the concrete figures to argue that off-cluster capacity planning is a real transferred burden on a process whose failure takes the whole data path down.
findings.evidence: [[llm-d-routerdocsoperationsmd-at-main-llm-dllm-d-router-github]] — roughly 7.5 cores idle at 100 model-serving pods; 4-6 GiB memory at 50-100 RPS with 1k output tokens, exceeding 20 GiB at 5k output tokens.
findings.recommendation: Add the figures inline to that sentence. One clause, no restructuring.

findings.location: Section 4D 'The gateway tier is moving the other way' and Section 7A Rule 4
findings.issue: The draft notes that off-Kubernetes an ORIGINAL_DST proxy has no endpoint list to fail open to, but does not note that the ecosystem default moved the other way — GIE v1.4.0 made FailOpen the InferencePool chart default, a posture available precisely because the proxy holds its own endpoint set. That is a concrete, dated cost of the recommended architecture that the draft currently leaves implicit.
findings.evidence: [[release-v140-kubernetes-sigsgateway-api-inference-extension-github]] — GIE v1.4.0 (2026-03-20) made FailOpen the default failure mode in the InferencePool Helm chart, changing prior fail-closed behaviour when the EPP is unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence (in §4D or Rule 4, whichever reads better) noting the v1.4.0 default shift and that the resilience it provides is structurally unavailable to a header-driven ORIGINAL_DST data plane, which is why the fallback cluster is a deliberate configuration item rather than an optional extra.
